en: In the *Daśottara-sūtra* it is said: "Thus have I heard: at one time...
[the Blessed One] will teach the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; which is meaningful and well-phrased."
He will proclaim the holy life—exclusive, complete, pure, and stainless—namely, the Dharma discourse called the *Daśottara*.
Listen well and attend closely; I shall speak the Dharma discourse called the *Daśottara*.

What is the Dharma discourse named *Daśottara*, which leads to Nirvāṇa, brings about the end of suffering, and releases one from all fetters? Mit_1.1 One single dharma is of great benefit: namely, heedfulness (*apramāda*) regarding wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*). Mit_1.2 One single dharma is to be cultivated: mindfulness directed toward the body (*kāyagatā smṛti*), accompanied by tranquility.
Mit 1.3 One dharma is to be fully understood: contact that is with-outflows and conducive to grasping.
Mit 1.4 One dharma is to be abandoned: the conceit "I am.
Mit 1.5 One dharma belongs to the side of decline: improper mental attention.
Mit 1.6: One dharma partakes of distinction: appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo manasikāra*).

Mit 1.7: One dharma is difficult to penetrate: the immediate concentration of mind (*ānantarya-cetasaḥ samādhiḥ*). Mit 1.8: One dharma is to be produced: the non-temporal [knowledge] (*asāmayikī* ...).
Mit_1.9 One dharma is to be directly known: all sentient beings subsist on nutriment. Mit_1.10 One dharma is to be realized: the unshakable liberation of the mind.

Thus, venerable ones, these ten dharmas are thus, not otherwise, real, true, suchness, as they really are, non-perverted, and non-erroneous; this is how they are, to be seen with right wisdom as they truly are.
They are to be seen.
Mit_2.1 There are two qualities that are of great benefit: mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Mit_2.2 There are two qualities that should be cultivated: tranquility and insight. Mit_2.3 There are two phenomena that should be fully understood: name and form.
Mit 2.4 Two dharmas are to be abandoned: ignorance and craving for existence.
Mit 2.5 Two dharmas belong to the side of decline: lack of shame and lack of dread.
Mit 2.6 Two dharmas belong to the side of distinction: shame and dread.
Mit 2.7 Two things are difficult to penetrate: the possible as the possible, and the impossible as the impossible.
Mit 2.8 Two things are to be produced: the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.

Mit 2.9 Two things are to be directly known: whatever cause and whatever condition lead to the defilement of sentient beings, and whatever cause and whatever condition lead to the purification of sentient beings.
Two qualities are to be witnessed: knowledge and liberation.
Thus, O Venerable Ones, these twenty qualities are such as they truly are, as before, up to being seen with right wisdom.
Mit 3.1: There are three qualities that are of great benefit: attending upon true persons, hearing the true Dharma, and proper mental attention.

Mit 3.2: There are three qualities to be cultivated: the three concentrations—the concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, the concentration without directed thought and with only sustained thought, and the concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought. Mit 3.3: There are three things to be fully understood: the three states of existence—existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and existence in the formless realm.
Mit 3.4 Three factors are to be abandoned: the three cravings—craving for sense-pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
Mit 3.5 Three factors belong to the side of decline: the three unwholesome roots—greed as an unwholesome root, hatred as an unwholesome root, and delusion as an unwholesome root.
Mit 3.6 Three factors belong to the side of distinction: the three wholesome roots—non-greed as a wholesome root, non-hatred as a wholesome root, and non-delusion as a wholesome root.

Mit 3.7: Three things are difficult to penetrate: three signs—the sign of concentration, the sign of the stability of concentration, and the sign of emergence from concentration. Mit 3.8: Three things are to be generated: the three gateways to liberation—emptiness, the wishless, and the signless.
Mit 3.9: Three things are to be fully understood: the three feelings—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Three qualities are to be realized: the three types of knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣya-vidyā*). Which three? The knowledge of one beyond training that realizes the recollection of former abodes; the knowledge of one beyond training that realizes the passing away and rebirth of beings;
and the knowledge of one beyond training that realizes the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Thus, venerable ones, these thirty factors are as previously described.

There are four factors that are of great benefit; they are the four wheels of gods and humans, by means of which gods and humans—being disciplined—attain growth and expansion in wholesome qualities. What are the four?

A suitable dwelling place, reliance upon virtuous persons, one’s own right application, and merit performed in the past—these four qualities are to be cultivated. There are four foundations of mindfulness. Which four? The foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body in the body; the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and phenomena in phenomena.

Mit 4.3: Four things are to be fully understood: the four nutriments. The first is physical food, both gross and subtle; the second is contact; the third is mental volition; and the fourth is consciousness. Mit 4.4: Four things are to be abandoned: the four graspings. Which four? Grasping at sensual pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at rules and observances, and grasping at a doctrine of self.

Mit_4.5 There are four factors conducive to decline: the four misfortunes. These are: failure in ethical discipline, failure in view, failure in conduct, and failure in livelihood. Mit_4.6 There are four factors conducive to distinction: the four successes. These are: success in ethical discipline, success in view, success in conduct, and success in livelihood.

Mit_4.7 There are four factors that are difficult to penetrate: the four noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

The noble truth of practice. (Mit_4.8) Four dharmas are to be produced: the four cognitions—the cognition of suffering, the cognition of origin, the cognition of cessation, and the cognition of the path.

(Mit_4.9) Four dharmas are to be fully understood: the four perceptions. Some perceive them as limited; some perceive them as exalted; some perceive them as immeasurable; [some perceive that] there is none...
Some perceive "something" as the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana).

There are four dharmas to be realized; there are four dharmas to be directly witnessed. There are dharmas to be realized by means of the body, there are those to be realized by means of mindfulness, there are those to be realized by means of the eye, and there are dharmas to be realized by means of wisdom.
Thus, venerable ones, these forty factors are such and not otherwise; as before, they are to be seen with right wisdom.
(Mit_5.1) Five factors are very helpful; five are the limbs of one who is preeminent. (Mit_5.1.1) Here, a monk has faith that is established in the Tathāgata, rooted, and firmly grounded...

By way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): this is the first limb of one who is preeminent. Furthermore, a monk [acts] toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*): this is the second limb of one who is preeminent.
Furthermore, a monk is free from illness, healthy by nature, and endowed with a digestive faculty that is well-balanced—

neither too hot nor too cold, unafflicted, and pleasant for the season— by which what he has eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper and easy digestion. This is the third factor of one who is preeminent.
Furthermore, a monk is powerful, firm in his exertion, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome qualities. This is the fourth factor of one who is preeminent.

There are five things to be fully understood: the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*). Which five? The aggregate of clinging to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Mit_5.44 Five dharmas are to be abandoned: the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill will (*vyāpāda*), sloth and torpor (*styānamiddha*), restlessness and remorse (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Mit_5.5 Five dharmas belong to the side of decline; they are the five fallow states of mind (*cetaḥkhila*). Which five? Here, venerable sirs, a monk is uncertain and doubtful regarding the Teacher; he does not... he does not have faith and does not find serene confidence...
And when he is censured by wise fellow-practitioners with goads of speech and goads of fingers, does he become angry toward those fellow-practitioners?

There are five qualities conducive to distinction: the five faculties. What are the five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

Five things are difficult to penetrate; there are five elements leading to deliverance. Venerable sirs, when that learned noble disciple recollects sensual pleasures, his mind does not enter into them, does not find satisfaction in them, does not settle upon them, is not liberated by them, and does not shrink back from them.

Mit_5.7.1.b … Or a bundle of sinews, when cast into the fire, dissolves and does not spread… Mit_5.7.1.c … For one who recollects sensual pleasures, the mind does not leap toward them, does not find clarity in them, does not settle upon them, and is not liberated; it dissolves… Mit_5.7.1.d He does not experience that feeling. This is the escape.

Just as with sensual desires, so too with ill-will and non-ill-will, harmfulness and non-harmfulness, form and the formless, the view of a self-existent body and the cessation of the view of a self-existent body—there is an escape.
Five things are to be produced: noble right concentration consisting of fivefold knowledge.
This first knowledge arises within him as he thinks: "This concentration is noble, free from worldly gain, and free from the basis of rebirth. *Majjhima Nikāya* 5.8.1.
"This concentration is practiced by noble persons, praised by the wise, and not censured by wise fellow-celibates"—thus a second knowledge arises within him.
"This concentration is peaceful, sublime, attained through tranquility, and reached through one-pointedness"—thus a third knowledge arises within him.
"This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant ripening in the future"—thus, his fourth knowledge arises internally.
Furthermore, "I shall enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully"—thus, his fifth knowledge arises internally. Intermediate Summary Verse:

The noble one, the non-worthless person, the peaceful one, and the one with mindfulness directed toward the present—these five qualities are to be fully understood. There are five bases of liberation. Which are the five?
In this case, either the Teacher teaches the dharmas to a monk, or some wise fellow-celibate who stands in the position of a teacher.

Just as his Teacher— or some wise fellow-celibate standing in the position of a teacher— teaches the dharmas, so too does he come to experience the meaning and experience the dharma within those teachings.
For one who thus experiences the meaning and experiences the Dharma, joy arises;

for one who is joyful, rapture is born; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; for one whose body is tranquil, one feels pleasure; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the first basis of liberation.

Mit 5.9.1.d: When a monk or a nun remains there, their unliberated mind becomes liberated, their unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, their undestroyed taints (*āsrava*) are destroyed, and they attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nirvana, which they had not yet attained.
Mit 5.9.2.a: Furthermore, in this case, neither the Teacher nor any other wise person standing in the position of a guru teaches the Dharma to the monk.
Furthermore, he recites aloud in detail the teachings exactly as they have been heard and mastered, even for his fellow celibates.

In whatever way he recites aloud in detail the teachings exactly as they have been heard and mastered, in that very way he comes to possess experiential realization of the meaning (*arthapratisaṃvedin*) and experiential realization of the phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvedin*) regarding those teachings. For him who possesses such experiential realization of the meaning...
For one who experiences the Dharma, joy arises as previously described; this is the second basis of liberation.

Furthermore, neither does a teacher teach him the Dharmas, nor does any wise fellow-celibate in the position of a guru, nor does he himself recite aloud in detail the Dharmas exactly as they were heard and mastered.
Moreover, he extensively elucidates for others those teachings exactly as they have been heard and exactly as they have been mastered.

In whatever way he extensively elucidates for others those teachings exactly as they have been heard and exactly as they have been mastered, in that very way he comes to possess a realization of the meaning (*arthapratisaṃvedin*) and a realization of the phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvedin*) regarding those teachings. For him who possesses this realization of the meaning...
For one who experiences the Dharma, joy arises, as described before; this is the third basis of liberation.

Furthermore, neither does his teacher teach him the Dharmas, nor does any wise companion in the holy life standing in the position of a guru, nor does he himself recite aloud in detail the Dharmas as they were heard and mastered.

Nor does he extensively proclaim to others the teachings as they were heard and as they were mastered; rather, Rohagata reflects upon, weighs, and examines the teachings as they were heard and as they were mastered while alone. Indeed, in whatever way Rohagata reflects upon, weighs, and [examines] the teachings as they were heard and as they were mastered while alone...

As he examines them in such a manner, he becomes one who experiences the meaning (*arthapratisaṃvedin*) and one who experiences the phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvedin*) regarding those phenomena. In him, who experiences the meaning and experiences the phenomena, joy arises as previously described;
this is the fourth basis of liberation (*vimuktyāyatana*).

Furthermore, neither does his teacher teach him the Dharma, nor does any other wise person acting as a spiritual mentor or fellow practitioner; nor does he himself recite aloud in detail the teachings exactly as they were heard and mastered, nor does he explain those teachings in detail to others exactly as they were heard and mastered.

When a monk, having gone alone into seclusion, reflects upon, weighs, and examines the teachings exactly as they have been heard and mastered— and furthermore, when he possesses a certain sign of concentration that is well-grasped, well-attended to, well-sustained, and well-penetrated— then [he attains stability].

In whatever way that monk has a particular sign of concentration that is well-grasped, well-attended to, well-sustained, and well-penetrated, in that very way he becomes one who experiences the meaning and experiences the phenomena regarding those teachings.
For one who thus experiences the meaning and experiences the Dharma, joy arises;

for one who is joyful, rapture is born; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; for one whose body is tranquil, one feels bliss; and for one who is blissful, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the fifth basis of liberation.

Mit_5.9.5.d When a monk or a nun abides [in this], their unliberated mind becomes liberated, their unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, their unabandoned taints (*āsrava*) are abandoned, and they attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, *nirvāṇa*, which they had not yet attained. Mit_5.10 Five qualities are to be realized: the five aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*): the noble aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).
Thus, venerable ones, these fifty factors are just as they were previously described, unerring and true.
There are six factors that cause one to be honored, and six factors that lead to endearment. What are the six?
"May my bodily action toward the Teacher and toward wise fellow-practitioners be established in friendliness."

This quality is conducive to harmony, creates affection, commands respect, and brings delight; it leads to endearment, reverence, esteem, cultivation, integration, concentration, freedom from conflict, absence of dispute, and one-pointedness of mind.
It is loving verbal action.
6.1.3 Loving mental action.
6.1.4 Regarding those gains that are righteous, obtained through the Dharma, and ultimately contained within or placed in a bowl— in such gains,
we shall be consumers in common with our wise fellow-celibates, not consuming them in secret.
This is a principle conducive to harmony, as before.

Those precepts which are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, unadulterated, well-undertaken, well-adopted, praised by the wise, and not censured—by means of such precepts, we shall come to share in the commonality of virtue together with our wise fellow-celibates. This is a principle conducive to harmony, as before.
"This noble view is leading to liberation, penetrative, and issues forth; it leads to the complete destruction of suffering and to the making of an end to suffering.
Through such a view, we shall come to share in the same view as our wise fellow-celibates.
This Dharma is conducive to harmony... [as before] ...and conduces to unification."
Six qualities are to be cultivated; there are six constant abidings. What are the six?
Here, a monk, having seen forms with the eye, is neither glad nor sad, but abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.

Having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, touched tangibles with the body, or cognized mental phenomena with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad, but abides in equanimity, mindful.
Being fully aware:
six things are to be thoroughly understood—the six internal sense bases. Which six? The eye as an internal sense base, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind as an internal sense base.
Mit 6.4 Six factors are to be abandoned: the six groups of craving. Which six? Craving born of eye-contact; craving born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.

Mit 6.5 Six factors lead to decline: the six types of lack of respect. Which six? One dwells without respect for the Buddha... and one has evil friends. Mit 6.6 Six factors lead to distinction: the six types of respect, as before.
Six things are difficult to penetrate; there are six elements leading to deliverance. Which six?

In this regard, venerable sirs, a monk might say: "I have cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced the concentration of the mind on loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetaḥsamādhi*), yet nevertheless, ill-will (*vyāpāda*) still persists, completely overwhelming my mind.
He should be told: "Do not speak thus. Why is that? Because it is impossible, it is out of the question, that while [the concentration on] loving-kindness...

If the concentration of mind on loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetaḥsamādhi*) is practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed, it is impossible that ill-will (*vyāpāda*) should persist by taking possession of the mind. This is not possible.

This concentration of mind on loving-kindness is the escape from all ill-will. In this regard, venerable ones, if someone were to say: "The concentration of mind on compassion (*karuṇā-cetaḥsamādhi*) has been practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed by me, yet harmful intent (*vihiṃsā*) still persists by taking possession of my mind," [that would be impossible].

"You should not speak thus. Why is that? It is impossible, it is out of the question, that when the concentration of the mind on compassion has been practiced, cultivated, and made much of, it will allow a mind of cruelty to persist by taking possession of the mind; such a thing cannot occur.
This concentration of the mind on compassion is the escape from all forms of cruelty.

In this regard, if someone were to say: "Although I have cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced the meditative concentration of a joyful mind, dissatisfaction still persists, overwhelming my mind," one should tell him:

"Do not speak thus. Why is that? It is impossible, it is out of the question, that dissatisfaction should persist, overwhelming the mind, when the meditative concentration of a joyful mind has been cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced; such a thing cannot occur.
This is the escape from all aversions, namely, the concentration of the mind on sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

Here, if someone were to say: "I have cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced the concentration of the mind on equanimity (*upekṣā*), yet sensual desire and ill-will still persist, completely overwhelming my mind," he should be told:
"Do not speak thus. Why is that? Because it is impossible and there is no occasion for the [defilements] to remain in one who possesses equanimity.

When the concentration of equanimity has been practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed, it is impossible that sensual desire and ill will would remain, having taken possession of the mind. This concentration of equanimity of the mind is the escape from all sensual desire and ill will.

"Suppose someone here were to say: 'I have cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced the signless concentration of mind, yet nevertheless my consciousness that follows signs remains, completely taking possession of my mind.
One should tell him: 'Do not speak thus. Why is that? Because it is impossible, it is out of the question, that while one is in the signless concentration of mind..."

When [this] has been cultivated, developed, and practiced extensively, consciousness that follows after signs will persist by completely taking possession of the mind; this is impossible. This signless concentration of mind is the escape from all consciousnesses that follow after signs. … [Mit 7.7] … Seven things are difficult to penetrate: the seven stations of consciousness. Which are they?

7.7.1 There are material beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings and certain gods; this is the first station of consciousness. 7.7.2 There are material beings who are diverse in body but uniform in perception, such as the gods of Brahmā’s retinue who were first produced; this is the second station of consciousness.
7.7.3 There are material beings who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the Ābhāsvara gods; this is the third station of consciousness.
Mit 7.7.4 There are beings possessing form who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Subhakṛtsna realm. This is the fourth station of consciousness.

Mit 7.7.5 There are beings without form who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, having attained the sphere of infinite space, dwell in the sphere of infinite space.
For example, there are beings belonging to the sphere of infinite space; this is the fifth station of consciousness.

There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, attain and abide in the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "consciousness is infinite"; for example, the gods belonging to the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is the sixth station of consciousness.

There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," dwell having attained the sphere of nothingness; such as the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness. This is the seventh station of consciousness.

Mit 7.8 Seven dharmas are to be produced: the seven requisites of concentration (*samādhipariṣkāra*). They are as follows: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.
Mit 7.9 Seven dharmas are to be fully understood: the seven faultless bases (*nirdoṣavastu*). Which are the seven?
In this case, a monk’s faith toward the Tathāgata becomes deeply rooted, established, and firmly grounded.
… Eight factors are of great benefit; they are eight conditions for the attainment in the future of wisdom and the holy life not yet attained.
Here, venerable ones, a monk dwells in dependence upon the Teacher, or upon some wise fellow-celibate who occupies the position of a teacher. …
...for the sake of attaining in the future that wisdom which has not yet been attained in the holy life; this is the first condition for the Dharma.
Furthermore, that monk from time to time obtains the opportunity to hear a discourse on the Dharma that is profoundly deep.

For the sake of attaining in the future that wisdom of the holy life which has not yet been attained—this is the second condition for the Dharma. Furthermore, having heard that Dharma, that monk becomes endowed with two kinds of seclusion: seclusion of body and seclusion of mind. For the sake of attaining in the future that wisdom of the holy life which has not yet been attained—this is the third condition for the Dharma.
Furthermore, a monk...
[leading to] the future fulfillment of the holy life as previously described. This is the fourth condition for the Dharma.
Furthermore, a monk...
… endowed with qualities that make him easy to speak to, for the sake of the holy life in the future, as before. This is the fifth condition pertaining to the Dharma.
Furthermore, a monk…
For the sake of obtaining in the future that wisdom of the holy life which has not yet been obtained—this is the sixth condition for the Dharma.
Furthermore, a monk dwells in the presence of the Teacher and delights in the Dharma; he frequently recites the Dharma...
[leading to] the future attainment of the holy life as before. This is the seventh condition for the Dharma.
Furthermore, a monk dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in the five aggregates of clinging: "This is form; this is the arising of form;

this is the passing away of form. Thus [he contemplates] feeling, thus perception, thus mental formations, thus consciousness: "This is consciousness; this is the arising of consciousness; this is the passing away of consciousness."
In the future, it will lead to the fulfillment of the holy life, as previously described. This is the eighth condition for the Dharma.
// Intermediate Summary Verse //
The Teacher and the Dharma...
these eight are the conditions for the Dharma. Eight qualities are to be cultivated: the Noble Eightfold Path; namely, right view and right intention.
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration as the eighth.
(Mit 8.3) Eight things are to be fully understood: the eight worldly conditions. Which eight? Gain and loss, fame and infamy, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
(Mit 8.4) Eight things are to be abandoned: the eight wrong factors. Namely, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, and wrong effort.
False mindfulness and false concentration—these eight factors belong to the side of decline. There are eight bases of laziness.
Here, a monk dwells in dependence upon a village or a town; having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he [enters the village].
Having taken [that very intention], he enters that same village or town for alms, thinking: "From this I shall obtain excellent food and drink as much as I need. It occurs to him:
"I have obtained excellent food and drink as much as I need. It occurs to him: "I have obtained it."

"Excellent food, both hard and soft, has been provided for as long as I desire. Yet my body is not strong; it is not fit for work nor capable of exertion. What if I were to lie down right now? He lies down right then and there. He does not strive to reach what has not been reached, to attain what has not been attained, or to realize what has not been realized. This is the first basis of laziness.

Furthermore, a monk dwells in dependence upon a village or a town. Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, he enters that very village or town for alms, thinking: "I shall not obtain sufficient excellent food, whether hard or soft. It occurs to him thus:

And having not obtained excellent food, whether hard or soft, in sufficient quantity, it occurs to him: "I have not obtained excellent food, whether hard or soft, in sufficient quantity; my body is not strong, nor is it fit for work or capable of exertion.
What if I were to lie down right now?"

He simply lies down as soon as he returns; he does not exert himself for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, or for the actualization of what has not been actualized. This is the second basis of laziness. Furthermore, a monk may have traveled along a road during the day, and it occurs to him: "Indeed, by me during the day..."
“I have come to the path, yet I am unable to proceed upon the path or to apply myself to the training of the Teacher. What if I were to do as before? This is the sixth basis of indolence.
Furthermore, a monk becomes afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. It occurs to him: “I am now afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill; it is possible that...”
This possibility exists that...
what if I were to [act] as before? This is the seventh basis of laziness.
Furthermore, another monk has recently emerged from meditation; it occurs to him: "I have now recently emerged from meditation. It is possible that..."
…there might be untimely death and the passing away [of the lifespan]. What if I were to do as before? This is the eighth basis of indolence.
There are eight factors conducive to distinction; there are eight bases for the exertion of vigor. What are the eight?
In this case, a monk dwells depending upon a village or a town. Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, he...
Having taken [this intention], he enters that very village or town for alms, thinking: "From this, I shall obtain excellent food and drink as much as I need. It occurs to him:
"And having obtained excellent food and drink as much as I need, it occurs to me: 'I have obtained [it].'"

"Excellent is the food, both hard and soft, as much as I require; my body is fit for exertion in spiritual practice. What if I were to strive right now? He strives right away for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, and for the direct witness of what has not yet been witnessed. This is the first basis for the arousal of energy.

Furthermore, a monk dwells in dependence upon a village or a town. Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robes, he enters that very village or town for alms, thinking: "I shall not obtain sufficient excellent food, both hard and soft. Then this thought occurs to him:

And when he does not obtain excellent food, whether hard or soft, in sufficient quantity, it occurs to him: "I have not obtained excellent food, whether hard or soft, in sufficient quantity. My body is strong and capable of exertion in the practice of abandonment; what if I were to exert myself right now?"

He exerts himself and strives for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, and for the direct witness of what has not yet been witnessed. This is the second basis for the arousal of energy.

Furthermore, a monk may have work to be done tomorrow. He thinks: "I must indeed do this work tomorrow; it is not possible for me both to do the work and to apply myself to the yoga of the Teacher’s instruction."
"What if I were to exert myself right now? He exerts himself right now for the sake of filling up what is broken or what is deficient;

he exerts himself for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, and for the manifestation of what has not yet been manifested. This is the third basis for the undertaking of vigor.

Furthermore, monks, it may happen that a monk has performed work during the day. It occurs to him: "I have indeed performed work during the day; I am unable both to do further work and to apply myself to the yoga of the Teacher's instruction. What if I were to exert myself right now?"

He exerts himself precisely for the sake of filling up what is broken or what is deficient; he exerts himself for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, and for the direct witness of what has not been directly witnessed. This is the fourth basis for the undertaking of vigor.
Furthermore, when a monk must travel on a journey tomorrow, it occurs to him: "By me indeed..."
"Tomorrow the path must be traveled, yet I am unable both to travel the path and to apply myself to the teaching of the Teacher.
What if I were to exert myself right now? Thus he exerts himself right now, as before; this is the fifth basis for the arousal of vigor.
Furthermore, another monk has arrived on the road during the day. It occurs to him: "I have indeed arrived on the road during the day;
it is not possible for me both to travel the road and to perform the sacrifice within the Teacher’s dispensation. What if I were to exert myself right now?"
He exerts himself precisely to fill up a crack or a fissure; he exerts himself as before. This is the sixth basis for the undertaking of vigor.
Furthermore, monks, a monk becomes afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. It occurs to him: "I am now afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. It is possible that..."
"What if I were to exert myself right now," as before.
This is the seventh basis for the arousal of energy. Furthermore, a monk has recently emerged from meditation; it occurs to him: "I have now recently emerged from meditation. It is possible that..."

"...there might be untimely death and the passing away [of my life]. What if I were to exert myself right now? He exerted himself right now as before. This is the eighth basis for the undertaking of vigor. Eight things are difficult to penetrate: the eight liberations.
Possessing form, one sees forms: this is the first liberation.
Being internally percipient of the formless, one sees external forms: this is the second liberation.
Realizing the beautiful liberation with the body and attaining it, one dwells therein: this is the third liberation.

Furthermore, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, a monk enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, perceiving "space is infinite," just as the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space do. This is the fourth liberation.

Furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "consciousness is infinite," just as the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is the fifth liberation.
Furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness, just as the gods...
Having attained the sphere of nothingness, this is the sixth liberation.

Furthermore, a monk, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, just as the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception do;
this is the seventh liberation.
Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a monk dwells having realized the cessation of perception and feeling with his own body;
this is the eighth liberation.
This Dharma is for one of few desires; it is not the Dharma for one of great desires.
This Dharma is for one who is content; it is not the Dharma for one who is discontented.
This Dharma is for one who is secluded; it is not the Dharma for one who delights in company, who finds pleasure in company, or who is devoted to the practice of delighting in company.

This Dharma is for one who has initiated vigor; this Dharma is not for one who is indolent. This Dharma is for one whose mindfulness is established; this Dharma is not for one whose mindfulness is lost.
This Dharma is for one who is concentrated; this Dharma is not for one who is unconcentrated.
This Dharma belongs to the wise; this Dharma does not belong to the one of poor wisdom.

This Dharma belongs to one who delights in the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), who rejoices in the absence of conceptual proliferation, and who is devoted to the practice of the yoga of delighting in the absence of conceptual proliferation. This Dharma does not belong to one who delights in conceptual proliferation, who rejoices in conceptual proliferation, and who is devoted to the practice of the yoga of delighting in conceptual proliferation.

Eight things are to be directly known; there are eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). Which eight? 1. Having the perception of internal forms, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered those forms, one knows them and sees them, and one possesses such a perception. This is the first base of mastery.

Mit_8.9.2 Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered those forms, one knows them and has mastered them, and one perceives thus. This is the second base of mastery. Mit_8.9.5 … Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster, just like a well-developed *umaka* flower...
Like a cloth from Vārāṇasī, even so,
one who is internally percipient of the formless sees external forms that are blue,
blue in color, appearing blue, and luminous with blue; having mastered those forms, one knows them and, having mastered them, sees them— such is his perception.
And it becomes thus. This is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Internally perceiving no form, one sees external forms that are yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster—just like a *karṇikāra* flower, or a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī that is perfectly dyed yellow. In this very way, internally perceiving no form...
One sees external forms as before; this is the sixth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

There are nine qualities that are of great benefit. What are the nine? They are the qualities preceded by the purification of vigor and generosity. Which are the nine? 1. Purification of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*).
Mit_9.1.2 Purity of mind; Mit_9.1.3 Purity of view;
Mit_9.1.4 Purity of relinquishment through self-control.
Mit_9.1.5 Purity of the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path; Mit_9.1.6 Purity of the knowledge and vision of the way of practice;
Mit_9.1.7 Purity of knowledge and vision.
Mit_9.1.8 Purity of wisdom;
Mit_9.1.9 Purity of liberation. Mit_9.2 Nine qualities should be cultivated, as well as nine qualities preceded by mental clarity. Which are the nine?
... nine factors to be fully known: the nine abodes of beings. What are the nine?
Mit_9.3.1 There are material beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings and certain gods. This is the first abode of beings.
Mit_9.3.2 There are material beings who are diverse in body but uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-realm who were first produced there. This is the second abode of beings.
Mit_9.3.3 There are material beings who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the Ābhāsvara gods. This is the third abode of beings.
Mit_9.3.4 There are material beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna gods. This is the fourth abode of beings.
Mit_9.3.5 There are material beings who are non-percipient and devoid of perception, such as the Unconscious Gods (asaṃjñisattva). This is the fifth abode of beings.

There are formless beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, having attained the base of infinite space through the thought "space is infinite," dwell therein— just as the gods who have reached the base of infinite space. This is the sixth abode of beings.

Mit_9.3.7 There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, dwell having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness; namely, the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is the seventh abode of beings. Mit_9.3.8 There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, dwell having attained the sphere of nothingness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever"; namely, the gods [who have reached the sphere of nothingness]. This is the eighth abode of beings.
Those who have reached the sphere of nothingness—this is the eighth abode of beings.

There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, dwell having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; namely, the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the ninth abode of beings.
Nine factors are to be abandoned.
… Nine unwholesome qualities lead to decline. There are nine bases of malice:
"He has done me harm, he is doing me harm, and he will do me harm"—these are the three bases of malice.
"He has done, is doing, and will do me harm"—this is another triad of objects for malice.
"He has done, is doing, and will do what is beneficial for my enemy"—this is another triad of objects for malice.
(Mit 9.6) There are nine factors conducive to distinction: the nine ways of dispelling malice.

"He has done me harm, he is doing me harm, he will do me harm... may it not be so"—thinking thus, he [removes] that resentment toward him. How could this be obtained? "May it be thus for me," [he thinks]; in this way, he dispels the present resentment. ... "He is my friend... desiring honor, desiring pleasure, desiring touch, desiring security..."

...this is its meaning: "He has done, is doing, or will do harm to her; may it not happen! Thus, for the sake of her, he dispels the resentment toward that [person]. How can this be obtained? [By thinking: "May it be thus for me," he dispels the present resentment arising from another.

Regarding that desire of an enemy for my harm, for what is unbeneficial, for suffering, for unpleasant contact, or for the lack of security— since this [enemy] has done, is doing, or will do such a thing to me,
and since it is not the case that "may this not happen," how can it be possible for him to obtain this wish: "May it be thus for me" regarding the future, or "May it be thus" regarding the present?
He dispels resentment.
There are nine grounds that are difficult to penetrate. When a monk [practices] in this way, he abandons the unwholesome.
He cultivates the wholesome.
A monk, by means of reckoning, abandons one thing;
by means of reckoning, he dispels one thing.
Having reckoned, he practices one dharma;
having reckoned, he endures one dharma. He generates nine dharmas that are not to be abandoned: the nine successive meditative abidings.
The first dhyāna,
the second dhyāna,
the third dhyāna.
The fourth dhyāna;
the sphere of infinite space;
the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The sphere of nothingness,
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and the cessation of perception and feeling.

Nine things are to be fully understood; nine things are to be realized. Thus, venerable ones, these ninety things are such as they are, not otherwise, not different, and so forth, up to: they are to be seen with right wisdom. Ten things are very helpful; ten are the things that provide protection.
Mit 10.1.1 Here, a monk is firmly established in faith... this is the first quality that provides a protector.
Mit 10.1.2 Furthermore, a monk dwells possessed of virtue, as before; this is the second quality that provides a protector.
Mit 10.1.3 Furthermore, a monk dwells with virtuous friends, as before; this is the third quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, a monk dwells in seclusion as before; this is the fourth quality that makes one a protector.

Furthermore, a monk dwells with aroused energy as before; this is the fifth quality that makes one a protector. Furthermore, a monk dwells possessed of mindfulness as before; this is the sixth quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, a monk dwells possessed of wisdom as previously described; this is the seventh quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, a monk is easy to speak to and is endowed with qualities that make him easy to speak to as previously described; this is the eighth quality that makes one a protector.

Furthermore, a monk is a lover of the Dharma and delights in the Dharma; he frequently proclaims the Dharma in the presence of the Teacher [and so forth]; this is the ninth quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore,

a monk who is untiring and endowed with diligence regarding those services that are to be performed for his fellow practitioners of the holy life, being one who acts and accomplishes them— this is the tenth quality that creates a protector.
Mit_10.2 Ten qualities are to be cultivated; there are ten things that are free from fever. What are the ten?

Mit_10.2.1 Through right view, wrong view is exhausted. Those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise for one on account of wrong view are exhausted by means of this [right] view, and through the condition of right view, they are eliminated.
Many wholesome qualities reach the fulfillment of their cultivation:
right intention and right speech.
Right action (samyakkarmānta), right livelihood (samyagājīva), and right effort (samyagvyāyāma).
Mit_10.2.7 Right mindfulness;
Mit_10.2.8 Right concentration;
Mit_10.2.9 Right liberation.

By means of right knowledge, false knowledge is exhausted. Those numerous evil and unwholesome states that arise for one through the condition of false knowledge cease, while numerous wholesome states arise through the condition of right knowledge and reach the fulfillment of their cultivation. (Mit 10.3) Ten things are to be fully understood: the ten material sense-bases (*rūpy-āyatana*). Which ten? They are as follows:
The sense-base of the eye; the sense-base of visible forms;
the sense-base of the ear.
The sense-sphere of sound,
the sense-sphere of the nose,
and the sense-sphere of odor.
The sense-base of the tongue;
the sense-base of tastes; the sense-base of the body.
Mit_10.3.10 The sense-sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). Mit_10.4 Ten factors are to be abandoned: the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) that obstruct the mind.
Mit_10.4.1 There is sensual desire for sensual pleasures; there is sensual desire for sensual pleasures. Regarding that which...

... whatever sensual desire there is for sense-pleasures, that too is an hindrance; whatever sensual desire there is for sense-pleasures, that too is an hindrance that does not conduce to direct knowledge, to awakening, or to Nirvāṇa.

There is ill-will and there is resentment. In this regard, whatever ill-will there is, that too is an hindrance; whatever cause for resentment there is, that too is an hindrance that does not conduce to direct knowledge or to awakening.

It does not conduce to Nirvana. There is sloth and there is torpor; therein, both that which is sloth is an hindrance, and that which is torpor is also an hindrance—it does not conduce to direct knowledge, nor to awakening, nor to Nirvana.

There is restlessness and there is remorse. In that regard, whatever restlessness there is, that too is an obscuration; whatever remorse there is, that too is an obscuration; it does not conduce to direct knowledge, nor to full awakening, nor to nirvāṇa.
There is doubt regarding wholesome states and there is doubt regarding unwholesome states. In that regard, [the doubt] regarding wholesome states...

Doubt regarding phenomena is also an obscuration; even doubt regarding unwholesome phenomena is an obscuration that does not lead toward higher knowledge, awakening, or nirvāṇa. (Mit 10.5) There are ten types of karma conducive to decline. There are ten unwholesome paths of action. Which are the ten? They are as follows:
1. Taking life, 2. taking what is not given, 3. sexual misconduct.
Mit_10.5.4 False speech; Mit_10.5.5 Slander; Mit_10.5.6 Harsh speech.
Mit_10.5.7 Frivolous speech;
Mit_10.5.8 Covetousness;
Mit_10.5.9 Malice.
10.5.10 Wrong view.
10.6 Ten factors conducive to distinction: the ten wholesome paths of action. Which ten? They are as follows:
10.6.1 Abstinence from taking life.
From taking what is not given,
from sexual misconduct,
and from false speech.
Abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous chatter.
Mit_10.6.8 Non-covetousness; Mit_10.6.9 Absence of ill-will;
Mit_10.6.10 Right view.
Mit_10.7 There are ten dharmas that are difficult to penetrate and ten noble abodes. What are the ten? Mit_10.7.1 The noble one is one who has abandoned five factors;
Mit_10.7.2 he is endowed with six factors.
One who guards the one,
one who relies on the four,
and one who has cast aside the individual truths.
10.7.6 One who has relinquished all longing; 10.7.7 one whose intentions are undisturbed;
10.7.8 one whose bodily formations are calmed.

With a mind well-liberated (suvimuktacitta), with wisdom well-liberated (suvimuktaprajña), he has dwelt as a solitary one, the Supreme Person (uttamapuruṣa). Ten qualities are to be produced; [as are] the ten spheres of totality (daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni).
Mit_10.8.1 Some perceive the "earth-totality," [extending] upwards, downwards, and across, non-dual and immeasurable.
Mit_10.8.2 The water-totality.
Mit_10.8.3 The fire-totality.
Mit_10.8.4 the air-totality; Mit_10.8.5 the blue-totality; Mit_10.8.6 the yellow-totality.
Mit_10.8.7 The entirely red; Mit_10.8.8 The entirely white;
Mit_10.8.9 The entirely space-infinity-sphere.

Mit_10.8.10 Some perceive the totality of the sphere of infinite consciousness as above, below, across, non-dual, and immeasurable. Mit_10.9 Ten things are to be directly known: the ten powers of the Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, claims his noble, preeminent position and turns the Brahma-wheel in the assembly.
He roars the true lion’s roar. What are the ten?
There are ten qualities to be realized: the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*). What are the ten? They are as follows:
the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Right intention,
right speech,
and right action.
Right livelihood,
right effort,
and right mindfulness.
Mit_10.10.8 Right concentration; Mit_10.10.9 Right liberation;
Mit_10.10.10 Right knowledge.
"Thus, venerable ones, these one hundred dharmas are such and not otherwise, as previously stated, up to: they are to be seen with right wisdom...
This is the Dharma discourse named 'The One Hundred and Ten. The Venerable Śāriputra said this, and those monks, their minds satisfied, rejoiced in what the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken."
